en: The Biography of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, translated by Kumārajīva, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna was born into the Brahmin caste in South India; he possessed natural brilliance and extraordinary insight.
Without needing to be told again,
while still among the nursing children,
he heard various brahmins reciting the four Vedas, each consisting of forty thousand verses.
The verse consists of thirty-two characters;
he recited its text while grasping its meaning.
Having reached the age of twenty, he was renowned for his brilliance, walking alone and peerless among all nations.
He thoroughly mastered astronomy, geography,
the *tuwei* and *miche* texts, as well as all various esoteric arts;
his three close friends were likewise paragons of their time.
They deliberated among themselves, saying:
"We have exhausted all the principles of the world that can open the way for the divine spirit and awaken one to the profound meaning."
Furthermore, what else could one seek for self-entertainment?
To indulge the passions and exhaust one's desires is the ultimate pleasure of a single lifetime.
Yet, such is the power of the various brahmins and practitioners.
"How could we obtain this without being princes or dukes?
Only through the art of invisibility can this pleasure be accomplished.
The four men looked at one another, their hearts in perfect accord.
They went together to a master of arts to seek the method for invisibility.
The master thought to himself:
"These four brahmins have achieved renown throughout the world and treat all living beings as mere blades of grass."
Now, for the sake of this art, you have condescended to come to me.
These brahmins possess talent and brilliance that are peerless in the world;
the only thing they do not know is this lowly practice.
"If I were to bestow it upon him,
he would surely abandon me once he had obtained it and could not be brought back under my influence.
For now, let him take the medicine for his use."
Not knowing that the medicine would run out and that he would surely come to be their teacher for all eternity,
[the Buddhas] each gave him a pill of green medicine and told him:
"In a quiet place, grind this with water."
"Use it to smear upon your eyelids, and your form shall be hidden;
no one will see you.
When Nāgārjuna ground this medicine, he recognized it immediately by its scent.
The proportions were exact, down to the smallest fraction of a grain, without any error.
He returned and informed the Medicine Master that the medicines he had obtained consisted of seventy kinds,
and their quantities were all precisely according to the prescription.
The physician asked, "By what means do you know this?
He replied, "Medicine has its own fragrance; how could one not know it?"
The Master immediately sighed in admiration and submission,
saying: "If even hearing of such a person is difficult,
how much more so is actually encountering them?"
"What is there to begrudge in my humble arts?
he said, and immediately bestowed them all upon them.
Having received the arts, the four men acted according to their own will with complete freedom.
He constantly entered the royal palace,
where the beautiful women therein were all subjected to his assault.
After more than a hundred days, a woman among the ladies of the inner court became pregnant.
Terrified, he reported this to the king, hoping to escape blame;
the king was greatly displeased, saying, "How can this be an auspicious sign? To have such a strange omen!"
He summoned his wise ministers to deliberate on this matter.
An elder among them spoke, saying:
"Generally, such matters are of two kinds."
Whether it be due to malevolent spirits or sorcery,
one may place fine dust at the various gates and have the officials guard them to block all passers-by.
If it is a sorcerer, their traces will manifest of themselves and they can be eliminated with military force;
if it is a malevolent spirit, it enters without leaving any trace.
"It can be extinguished by means of a technique.
He then commanded the gatekeeper to test him according to the prescribed method.
Upon seeing the tracks of four men, he reported this urgently to the king.
The king led several hundred strongmen into the palace and closed all the gates.
He ordered the strongmen to brandish their blades and strike at empty air; the three men died instantly.
Only Nāgārjuna remained there, restraining his body and holding his breath by the side of the king's head.
Seven feet from the king's head was where the sword could not reach.
At that moment, he finally realized that desire is the root of suffering and the source of all calamities.
The ruin of virtue and the endangerment of one's person both arise from this.
He then made a vow to himself, saying:
"If I am able to escape, I shall go to a śramaṇa and receive the dharma of renunciation."
Having entered and exited the mountains, he went to a Buddhist stupa to leave the household life and receive the precepts.
Within ninety days, he had completely recited the Tripitaka;
yet when he sought other scriptures, he found no place where they were available.
He then entered the Snow Mountains, where there was a stūpa.
Inside the stūpa was an elderly bhikṣu,
who gave him Mahāyāna sūtras.
Although he recited, received, and took delight in it, even though he understood its true meaning, he had not yet attained mastery;
he traveled through various countries seeking other sūtras,
searching throughout Jambudvīpa without success.
The non-Buddhist masters and the tenets of the śramaṇas were all utterly defeated.
A disciple of the non-Buddhists said to him,
"My teacher is an omniscient one."
Now you are a disciple of the Buddha.
Is the way of discipleship—relying upon and receiving instruction from others—not yet sufficient?
If it is not yet sufficient in even one respect, then one is not omniscient.
When their arguments were exhausted and their positions defeated, they immediately gave rise to a mind of deviant pride and thought to themselves:
"In the worldly dharmas, there are many paths and gateways."
Although the Buddhist scriptures are subtle, when examined through reasoning, there are points that remain incomplete;
within those incomplete portions, one may infer and elaborate upon them so as to awaken later students without contradicting the underlying principle.
Since there is no error regarding this matter, what fault could there be?
Having reflected on this, he immediately desired to carry it out;
he established a teacher’s instructions and precepts, and further fashioned robes.
He caused them to adhere to the Buddha-dharma with minor variations.
Desiring to remove the sentiments of the assembly and demonstrate that he did not accept [their] training, he chose an auspicious day and time at which he would bestow [the precepts].
The disciples received the new precepts and donned new robes.
While he was alone in a crystal chamber in a quiet place,
the Great Dragon Bodhisattva, seeing him in such a state, felt pity and compassion for him;
he immediately took him up and entered the sea.
Within the palace, he opened the treasuries of the seven precious gems and unfurled the caskets of the seven precious flowers,
bestowing upon him the immeasurable, wondrous Dharma of the various profound and extensive Vaipulya sūtras.
After Nāgārjuna had studied for ninety days, he attained profound understanding in many areas;
his mind entered deeply, and he realized the actual benefit.
Knowing this in his heart, Nāgārjuna asked him:
"Have you finished reading all the scriptures? He replied,
"The scriptures within your various cases are so numerous and immeasurable that they cannot be exhausted."
The number of those who can read it is ten times that of Jambudvīpa.
The dragon said,
"It is like all the scriptures found within my palace."
In various places, such instances are too numerous to count.
Once Nāgārjuna had attained the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) of all sūtras and deeply entered the two types of patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
he returned to South India and sent [the texts] out.
He extensively propagated the Buddha-dharma and subdued the non-Buddhists.
He widely elucidated the Mahāyāna by composing one hundred thousand verses of *upadeśa*,
and further composed five thousand verses of the *Śrī-saṃghāṭa-sūtra-śāstra* (Treatise on Adorning the Buddha-way).
The *Mahāmaitrī-upāya-śāstra* in five thousand verses and the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* in five hundred verses caused the Mahāyāna teachings to flourish extensively throughout India.
Furthermore, he composed the *Abhayapaddhati* (The Treatise on Fearlessness) in one hundred thousand verses;
from within it, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* emerged.
At that time, there was a Brahmin.
Being well-versed in incantations and wishing to contend with Nāgārjuna to prove his own superiority,
he informed the King of India:
"I am able to subdue this bhikṣu."
"The King should verify this.
The King said,
"You are utterly foolish."
This Bodhisattva’s brilliance vies with the light of the sun and moon, and his wisdom shines alongside the minds of the sages.
Why do you not show humility and dare to fail to revere him?
The brāhmaṇa said,
"Your Majesty is a wise man; why do you not test this by means of reason,
instead of suppressing and humiliating him?"
When the king saw that his words were so earnest, he requested Nāgārjuna on his behalf.
At dawn, they sat together in the main hall of the palace to listen;
the brahmin arrived later.
He then performed a spell before the palace to create a vast, long, and pure great pond.
Within it was a thousand-petaled lotus flower,
upon which he sat and boasted to Nāgārjuna.
"Sitting on the ground, you are no different from a beast,
yet you wish to debate with me, a pure and great virtuous scholar, upon this noble flower. At that time,
Nāgārjuna also used a spell to transform himself into a six-tusked white elephant.
He walked across the surface of the pond toward his flower-seat;
with his trunk, he coiled it up, lifted it high, and hurled it to the ground,
causing the brahmin’s waist to be injured.
Exhausted and prostrate, I take refuge in Nāgārjuna.
Having failed to measure my own capacity, I have brought disgrace upon the Great Master;
I pray that you will compassionately accept me and dispel my ignorance.
Furthermore, the King of South India ruled over all the various states and placed his trust in heterodox paths;
not a single śramaṇa or son of the Śākyas was permitted to be seen.
People from near and far throughout the kingdom were all converted to his way.
Nāgārjuna thought to himself:
"If a tree's root is not cut down, its branches will not fall.
If a sovereign does not transform his people, the Way will not prevail."
The laws and regulations of that kingdom required the royal household to provide funds to hire men for night watch and guard duty.
Nāgārjuna then responded to the recruitment and served as their commander.

Carrying halberds, he led the vanguard, bringing order to the ranks and disciplining the divisions; his authority was established without the need for severity, and his commands were effectively carried out.
The Dharma was not yet manifest, yet sentient beings followed it.
The King highly praised this and asked, "Who is this person?"
The attendant replied,
"This man has responded to the call for service; he neither eats from the granary nor takes money,
yet he is so respectful and diligent in his duties, and so well-versed in them."
Not knowing his intention— what he sought or what he desired—
the king summoned him and asked: "Who are you?"
He replied, "I am an omniscient one.
The king was greatly startled and asked:
A person of all-knowledge appears but once in many generations.
You say yourself what you are; how do you verify this?
He replied:
"If you wish to know where wisdom resides, Your Majesty should question the speaker.
The king then thought to himself, "I am a master of wisdom and a great debater; if I question him, I shall be able to humble him."
Even this was not enough to name it; that on a single occasion he did not act otherwise was no small matter.
Had he not asked, it would have been a humiliation.
After hesitating for a long time, he could not help but ask.
"Deva, what are you doing now?
Nāgārjuna replied,
"Deva, I am currently at war with the asuras."
When the king heard these words,
he was like a person choking, unable to spit it out and yet unable to swallow it down.
If one desires to speak of what is not [the case], there is nothing with which to verify it;
if one desires to speak of what is [the case], there is no phenomenon by which it can be clarified—
this is so even before a word has been spoken.
Nāgārjuna spoke again:
"This is no empty discourse nor a mere attempt to seek victory;
Your Majesty, please wait a short while."
As soon as he had finished speaking, a sign appeared immediately;
from the sky there began to fall a continuous succession of shields, spears, and weapons.
The King said:
"Although spears, halberds, lances, and pikes are weapons of war,
why must you know that this is a battle between the devas and the asuras?
Nāgārjuna said:
"Rather than relying on empty words, it is better to verify through actual facts.
Having said this, the hands, feet, fingers, ears,
and noses of the asuras descended from the sky.

Furthermore, he caused the king, his ministers, the common people, and the assembly of brahmins to see the two armies arrayed against each other in the sky, which had been cleared of all obstructions.
The king then prostrated himself, submitting to the transformative power of the Dharma.
Within the palace hall were ten thousand brahmins.
They all discarded their tied-up hair and received the precepts of accomplishment.
At that time, there was a teacher of the Hīnayāna who constantly harbored resentment and malice.
As Nāgārjuna was about to depart from this world, he asked him, saying:
"Do you wish for me to remain long in this world?"
He replied,
"In truth, this is not what I desire.
He then withdrew into a quiet room and did not emerge for several days.
The disciple broke open the door to look inside;
[the master] had already cast off his mortal coil and departed.
From the time he left this world until the present day—
When he had first passed his hundredth year,
the various kingdoms of South India erected temples for him and venerated him as they would a Buddha.
His mother gave birth to him beneath a tree.
It is therefore called Ajapada;
Ajapada is the name of a tree, and it was by means of this tree that the path was established.
Therefore, he was given the character "Dragon" (Nāga) as part of his name and titled Nāgārjuna. According to the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (The Tradition of the Transmission of the Dharma),
he was the thirteenth patriarch.
By means of elixirs and divine medicines, he manifested a long life of over two hundred years.
He upheld the Buddha-dharma,
and the number of people he delivered cannot be calculated.
As stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*,
according to the *Biography of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna*.
